articles.excerpt: The first time an alert went off on my nightstand at 1:40 a.m., it was a fire warning. We had decided earlier to stay and fight as we were well prepared, but as that slight sense of relief set in, I started to think about communicating that decision with my family in the city. I grabbed the phone, squinted at 11% battery, and spent the next four minutes trying to remember whether my mum's landline number was saved anywhere other than in that phone. That's when I realised that it wasn't. A family emergency plan works best when it exists in two places at once, because the pocket version fails in exactly the conditions that make you need it. Batteries drain. Towers get congested. Cloud storage needs a connection you may not have. Your phone is still the fastest thing you own for warnings and check-ins, and none of that changes the fact that a printed sheet in a kitchen drawer works at 3 a.m. with the power out. Name one out-of-state contact and put that number in every phone and on a wallet card for each person. CDC advises storing at least 1 gallon of water per person, per day for 3 days, with two weeks as the goal. The surveillance problem nobody predicted About half of parents in the US now use location-tracking apps to monitor their teenagers' movements, according to a study published in the Journal of Family Psychology. A further 14% of parents in the study were tracking their children without the child's knowledge - the monitoring was happening without the teen being aware of it at all. That second statistic is worth sitting with. One in seven families using these apps are doing so secretly.
